Taking this up would commit you to treating the ambiguity of agreements, not just the division of labor, as the object of repair. Concretely, it asks you to produce at least one written, testable agreement for a single chore, including a trigger and an observable standard, and to try a default rule for schedule changes before concluding that negotiation has failed. That is a proposed application, not a claim that it will work in your flat.

It also commits you to distinguishing what you can observe from what you infer: whether the avoiding friend is avoiding the topic, the conflict, or you is not settled by their absence from a conversation. If you later rely on this account, you would need to keep that distinction alive rather than treating avoidance as evidence of bad faith. The emphasis on one friction point and a low-pressure check-in is a scope choice; it deliberately leaves open whether a larger household meeting, a formal rota, or renegotiating standards by preference would be better. Those are unresolved here because I do not know your flatmates' constraints or how decisions have gone before.

The criticism I would invite is that this approach may be too procedural for a situation where the real issue is a damaged friendship, or too optimistic about a written agreement when one person has already withdrawn. If that criticism holds, the recommendation to shift from chores to whether shared decisions are possible at all becomes the more important part, and the three-part agreement becomes a smaller diagnostic step rather than the solution. I am not claiming the written agreement will be respected, only that it makes the disagreement about meaning visible enough to discuss. What I currently propose to take up is the sequencing: one testable micro-agreement, one default adjustment rule, one check-in, then reassess. entries.verbatim: If this is taken up, the load-bearing claim is that the four strands can be usefully separated, and in particular that the recurring conflict is more about unstable referents for past agreements than about contested fairness. That is a conjecture from a single account; testing it would mean trying the written-record proposal for a bounded period and seeing whether the "what did we agree" arguments actually decrease, as distinct from arguments about the distribution itself continuing. A second thing I am proposing to act on is approaching the avoidant flatmate with a narrowed, one-topic frame and an explicit offer to renegotiate; if that makes participation worse or produces no engagement, the inference I would draw is about the household's current coordination capacity, not about that person's character, though the distinction may be hard to maintain in practice. The narrower fallback — each person owning their own tasks with reduced mutual dependency — is a consequence I would accept as a real outcome rather than a failure of the attempt above, but it has costs I have not weighed, notably that shared spaces and shared purchases stop being anyone's clear responsibility. The strongest criticism available to anyone reading this is that a procedural fix may be treating a symptom: if the underlying issue is that one person rejects the distribution, no amount of writing things down resolves it, and my framing would then be misdirected. I have not resolved that; I only flag that the written-record proposal is most plausible where the problem is interpretation and weakest where it is non-acceptance. entries.verbatim:
Taking this up would involve proposing a reset conversation framed as fixing the process rather than relitigating past chores; drafting a one-page charter with concrete definitions, owners, deadlines, and swap rules; running it as a two-to-four week trial; and holding a short review. It depends on all three being willing to try, or at least on the two willing flatmates not using it as a weapon against the third. If the avoiding friend will not join a group meeting, I would first try a private low-pressure conversation and an async written option; if that fails, the proposal narrows to what you and the other willing flatmate can do and to deciding whether to stay.

The claim that written specificity reduces disputes is a prediction, not a guarantee. It should be judged by whether arguments become less frequent and more concrete, not by whether everyone suddenly likes chores. I would criticize this approach as potentially bureaucratic, and as possibly over-focusing on fairness accounting while missing burnout, stress, or mental health. Unresolved: what to do if standards differ irreconcilably, whether a paid cleaner is acceptable, and how long to persist before treating the living arrangement itself as the problem. I would not treat the charter as a truth certificate or a permanent constitution; I would revise or drop it if it increases resentment or if the flatmates will not honestly use it.
